newsitem.title: JAPAN: Veteran politician becomes Japan finance minister.
newsitem.headline: Veteran politician becomes Japan finance minister.

text.p: Japan's new Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka could face a particularly tricky task on top of the already daunting demands of the job -- trimming the power of the mighty agency.
The Finance Ministry, under fire for policy missteps and scandals, is a prime target for reforms pledged by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
A veteran conservative politician who leads one of the biggest factions in the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), Mitsuzuka held a number of key cabinet and party posts in the 1980s.

This included a brief stint as foreign minister and a longer spell at the Trade Ministry, during which in trade talks with the United States and other countries he took a realistic line, promising only what he thought he could deliver.

Among the many domestic agenda items the new minister must address are whether to craft a stimulative supplementary budget for the fiscal year to March 1997, the drafting of next year's budget, reform of the tax and pension systems, Japan's huge budget deficit and lurking financial system woes.
Top of his international agenda will be the scheduled resumption next week of Japan-U.S. talks over deregulation in Tokyo's insurance market.
The two sides have set a December 15 deadline for settling the dispute over implementation of a 1994 pact.

Washington wants Tokyo to deregulate its life and non-life insurance sectors before opening up its "third sector" niche market for nursing and accident healthcare, where U.S. insurers have a strong foothold.
"We want a tough negotiator who can bring the insurance trade talks to a successful conclusion," said a senior Finance Ministry official before the appointment of the new minister.

On the domestic front, Mitsuzuka -- a member of the LDP's old guard -- may use some of his experience in the late 1980s break-up of debt-ridden Japan National Railways when he deals with proposals to trim the power of his own ministry.

The ruling coalition unveiled a plan in September to reform the ministry, including the creation of an independent body to assume the supervisory and regulatory powers through which the ministry has exercised control over the financial industry.
The LDP and others have also proposed that the ministry be deprived of its monopoly over the budget-drafting process and that this function be given to the Prime Minister's Office.
Mitsuzuka grabbed the spotlight a decade ago when, as transport minister, he pushed for the privatisation and break-up of the national railways.
Ironically, however, he now inherits the legacy of that privatisation -- massive debts worth almost 28 trillion yen ($250 billion).
Like Hashimoto, Mitsuzuka, 69, is a keen practitioner of the Japanese art of Kendo, or medieval fencing. He is an avid reader and has written several books on politics and railways. ($1=112 yen)
